rationale: Behind the BSB's "It is I" (14:27) stand two Greek words, egō eimi, "I am," in every Greek edition Biblehub lists. Swete's Septuagint renders God's answer in Exodus 3:14 as Egō eimi ho ōn, "I am the One who is," which the BSB renders from the Hebrew as "I AM WHO I AM." So the English hides the overlap, and the Greek overlap is only two common words. In context they are also the ordinary way to say "it's me" to men who have just cried, "It's a ghost!" (14:26). Matthew gives no formula and does not name Moses, so the type at most is allusion. The label is plausible, not strong, because named readers argue it and named readers doubt it. Jerome (in the Catena Aurea) offers it as one of two possibilities: either the disciples could recognize Jesus by His voice, "or they might know that it was He who had spoken to Moses." Richard Hays, as reported by Derek Rishmawy, holds that the same words in Mark 6:50 "should probably be heard, then," as an echo of Exodus 3:14, drawing that from Job 9 and Mark's "pass by," which Matthew lacks; in Hays's own words as Rishmawy quotes them, the phrase "serves to underscore the claim of divine identity" in that story. Ian Paul writes that it "is not very clear from Matthew's account" whether to hear the divine name, "not least since this phrase is the natural one a person would use to give reassurance about their identity." Andrew Perriman would "dismiss the references to Exodus as tenuous." Isaiah 43:10 and 51:12, where the Septuagint has egō eimi near a call not to fear, were considered and not authored (see the lesson's Teach-Back 5).
